# OD matrices and spatial flows {#sec-m3-matrizes} The origin–destination matrix is the central structure of transport modelling. This chapter deals with three things: how to store it without wasting memory, how to turn it into geometry for the map, and how to compute indicators from it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(sf) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(ggplot2) library(Matrix) ``` ::: ## Long format and matrix format An OD matrix can be represented in two ways, and converting between them is routine: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} od_longo <- data.frame( origem = c("AM", "AM", "PA", "SP", "PR"), destino = c("SP", "PR", "MA", "AM", "AM"), toneladas = c(1200, 450, 980, 310, 120) ) od_largo <- od_longo |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = destino, values_from = toneladas, values_fill = 0) od_matriz <- as.matrix(od_largo[, -1]) rownames(od_matriz) <- od_largo$origem od_matriz #> SP PR MA AM #> AM 1200 450 0 0 #> PA 0 0 980 0 #> SP 0 0 0 310 #> PR 0 0 0 120 ``` ::: The long format is better for storing, filtering and joining; the matrix format is what models consume. Note the asymmetry: the flow AM→SP (1200) is not the same as SP→AM (310). That is the feature that distinguishes an OD matrix from a distance matrix. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # margins: production and attraction data.frame( zona = rownames(od_matriz), emitido = rowSums(od_matriz) ) |> dplyr::full_join( data.frame(zona = colnames(od_matriz), atraido = colSums(od_matriz)), by = "zona" ) |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.numeric), \(x) tidyr::replace_na(x, 0)), saldo = atraido - emitido) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Sparse matrices In a real OD matrix, most cells are zero: each zone relates to few others. Storing all the zeros wastes memory explosively. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 5000 # zones # dense matrix: stores n² values memoria_densa <- n^2 * 8 / 1024^3 # in GB (double = 8 bytes) round(memoria_densa, 2) #> [1] 0.19 ``` ::: A 5,000 × 5,000 matrix takes about 0.2 GB; with 20,000 zones (the number of census tracts in a metropolitan region) it would be more than 3 GB just to store zeros. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1) n_pares <- 50000 # only 0.2% of the pairs have flow esparsa <- Matrix::sparseMatrix( i = sample(n, n_pares, replace = TRUE), j = sample(n, n_pares, replace = TRUE), x = round(rlnorm(n_pares, 4, 1), 1), dims = c(n, n) ) format(object.size(esparsa), units = "MB") #> [1] "0.6 Mb" dim(esparsa) #> [1] 5000 5000 ``` ::: A few megabytes instead of hundreds. And the usual operations work as normal: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} soma_linhas <- Matrix::rowSums(esparsa) soma_colunas <- Matrix::colSums(esparsa) c(total = sum(esparsa), pares_com_fluxo = length(esparsa@x), densidade = round(length(esparsa@x) / (n * n), 5)) #> total pares_com_fluxo densidade #> 4505842.800 49947.000 0.002 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # back to the long format, only with the pairs that have flow longo <- summary(esparsa) |> as.data.frame() |> dplyr::rename(origem = i, destino = j, fluxo = x) head(longo, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} nrow(longo) #> [1] 49947 ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip} Travel time matrices from `r5r` and `dodgr` already come in the long format, with one row per pair. It is the "natural" sparse form. Convert to `sparseMatrix` when you need matrix algebra (trip distribution, gravity models); keep it as a `data.frame` when the work is filtering, aggregating and mapping. ::: ## From OD matrix to spatial flow The desire line map is the most recognisable representation of an OD matrix. Building it takes three steps: the zones' coordinates, lines between the pairs, and a visual scale that does not lie. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} zonas <- data.frame( zona = c("AM", "PA", "MA", "PR", "SP"), lon = c(-60.02, -48.50, -44.30, -49.27, -46.63), lat = c( -3.10, -1.46, -2.53, -25.43, -23.55) ) |> sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4674) # generic function: OD table + zone points -> desire lines od_para_linhas <- function(od, pontos, col_origem = "origem", col_destino = "destino", col_id = "zona") { xy <- sf::st_coordinates(pontos) idx <- setNames(seq_len(nrow(pontos)), pontos[[col_id]]) io <- idx[od[[col_origem]]] id <- idx[od[[col_destino]]] geom <- Map(\(a, b) sf::st_linestring(rbind(xy[a, ], xy[b, ])), io, id) |> sf::st_sfc(crs = sf::st_crs(pontos)) sf::st_sf(od, geometry = geom) } linhas <- od_para_linhas(od_longo, zonas) linhas ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arquivo <- "dados/brutos/uf_br.gpkg" if (!file.exists(arquivo)) { ufs <- geobr::read_state(year = 2020, showProgress = FALSE) sf::st_write(ufs, arquivo, quiet = TRUE) } ufs <- sf::st_read(arquivo, quiet = TRUE) ggplot() + geom_sf(data = ufs, fill = "grey97", colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.2) + geom_sf(data = linhas |> dplyr::arrange(toneladas), aes(linewidth = toneladas, alpha = toneladas), colour = "#1a5b8a") + geom_sf(data = zonas, size = 2, colour = "#0d3b5c") + scale_linewidth_continuous(range = c(0.3, 3), name = "Tonnes") + scale_alpha_continuous(range = c(0.35, 0.9), guide = "none") + theme_void(base_size = 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Desire lines: width proportional to the flow](m3-05-matrizes_files/figure-html/fig-desejo-1.png){#fig-desejo width=1200} ::: ::: Four representation decisions worth discussing with whoever will read the map: 1. **Width proportional to the flow** is the convention. With very skewed flows (the normal case), use a square-root or logarithmic scale, otherwise the largest line covers the map. 2. **Sorting from smallest to largest** (`arrange(toneladas)`) makes the large lines drawn on top, not hidden. 3. **Transparency** helps when many lines overlap. 4. **Filtering** is legitimate: showing the 30 largest flows and saying that they represent X% of the total usually communicates better than a thousand unreadable lines. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # ready-made alternatives for the same task stplanr::od2line(flow = od_longo, zones = zonas) # straight lines from the OD table stplanr::od2odf(od_longo, zonas) # coordinates of the pairs ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## A straight line is not a route The desire line shows **origin, destination and volume**, not the path. To represent the flow on the actual infrastructure (a highway, a shipping route), you need to route each pair and add up the flows per segment: the **assignment**. The result is a network loading map, in which the width sits on the road, not in the air. That is what the `flownet` package and the `stplanr::overline()` function do, and what we come back to in module 4. ::: ## Aggregating and subsetting a matrix Two routine operations: aggregating zones into larger regions and separating internal flows from external ones. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} regiao <- c(AM = "Norte", PA = "Norte", MA = "Nordeste", PR = "Sul", SP = "Sudeste") od_longo |> dplyr::mutate(reg_o = regiao[origem], reg_d = regiao[destino]) |> dplyr::summarise(toneladas = sum(toneladas), .by = c(reg_o, reg_d)) |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = reg_d, values_from = toneladas, values_fill = 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} od_longo |> dplyr::mutate(tipo = dplyr::if_else(origem == destino, "internal", "external")) |> dplyr::summarise(toneladas = sum(toneladas), pares = dplyr::n(), .by = tipo) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Indicators from the matrix ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # distance between the zones (in km), from the geometry d_km <- sf::st_distance(zonas) |> units::set_units(km) |> as.numeric() |> matrix(nrow = nrow(zonas), dimnames = list(zonas$zona, zonas$zona)) od_ind <- od_longo |> dplyr::mutate( dist_km = d_km[cbind(origem, destino)], tku = toneladas * dist_km ) od_ind |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku)) |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(dist_km, tku), \(x) round(x, 1))) |> knitr::kable() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |origem |destino | toneladas| dist_km| tku| |:------|:-------|---------:|-------:|---------:| |AM |SP | 1200| 2691.3| 3229587.1| |AM |PR | 450| 2736.2| 1231282.6| |SP |AM | 310| 2691.3| 834310.0| |PA |MA | 980| 481.7| 472022.7| |PR |AM | 120| 2736.2| 328342.0| ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # aggregate indicators od_ind |> dplyr::summarise( toneladas = sum(toneladas), tku = sum(tku), distancia_media_km = round(sum(tku) / sum(toneladas), 1) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: The **average haul distance** (TKU ÷ tonnes) is an indicator that sums up the matrix in one number and lets you compare modes, years and scenarios: it is how far, on average, each tonne travels. In the following case study, we take the opposite route: we start from the TKU published by ANTAQ and estimate the tonnage.
